desc:
In one step you may insert any lowercase letter at any position of the string s (the front, the back or between two letters). Return the minimum number of insertions needed to turn s into a palindrome.

For example, "abcba" is already a palindrome, so the answer is 0; "ab" needs 1 insertion ("aba"); "mbadm" needs 2 insertions (for example "mbdadbm").
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Look at the two outermost letters of the string. What happens if they are equal? What if they differ?
Let f(i, j) be the answer for the piece s[i..j]. If s[i] == s[j], those two letters already mirror each other, so f(i, j) = f(i+1, j-1).

If they differ, you must insert one letter to mirror either s[i] or s[j]: f(i, j) = 1 + min(f(i+1, j), f(i, j-1)). Fill the table by increasing length (or by decreasing i); an empty or single-letter piece costs 0.
editorial: Define dp[i][j] as the fewest insertions that make s[i..j] a palindrome. Single letters and empty pieces cost 0. If the end letters are equal, nothing is needed for them and dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1]. Otherwise one end letter has no mirror; inserting its copy on the opposite side costs one step and leaves a smaller piece, giving 1 + min(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
The answer is dp[0][n-1]. There are O(n2) states and each is computed in O(1), so time and space are O(n2); the table can be reduced to O(n) memory by keeping only the rows that are needed.

Equivalent view: the letters you do not need to insert for are exactly a longest palindromic subsequence of s, so the answer equals n minus the length of that subsequence. Every other letter needs one inserted mirror partner.
